**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

You already do this. When you hit a word you do not know, you keep reading and you often work it out. This week you learn the moves you were already making, so you can use them on purpose.

1. Read **The Words Around the Word**.
2. Learn the words in **Clue Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Four Kinds of Clue** chart where you can see it.
4. Sort the cards in **Which Clue Is It?**
5. Say the **Word Detective Frames** out loud with a partner.
6. Take **Word Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Four Clues**.
8. Read **Word Questions Kids Ask** — one answer says when to give up and look it up.
9. Finish with **Design: A Clue Hunt for a Reading Buddy**.

Your job this week: catch yourself working out one real word while reading, and tell somebody how you did it. 🔍

from:
## The Words Around the Word

Read this: *The path was so narrow that we had to walk single file.*

Suppose you did not know **narrow**. You would still have a good guess. If people have to walk one behind the other, the path must be thin. You did not look anything up. The sentence told you.

That is what a **context** **clue** is. The words around a word hint at what it means. You have been doing it since you were small.

There are four kinds worth knowing by name.

Sometimes the writer just tells you. *A glacier, a huge slow-moving river of ice, carved this valley.* That is a **definition** clue, and it is the easiest one.

Sometimes you get cases instead. *She packed produce: apples, carrots, and lettuce.* Nobody defined produce, but the **example** clue shows you it means fruits and vegetables.

Sometimes a nearby word means almost the same thing. *He was furious. I had never seen him so angry.* Angry is a **synonym**, and it hands you the meaning.

Sometimes the sentence swings the other way. *The room was not tidy; it was a shambles.* The little word not tells you a shambles is the opposite of tidy. That is an **antonym** clue.

Watch for **signal** words. Or, that is, and such as often bring a definition or an example. But, however and instead often bring an opposite.

The word itself can help too. A **prefix** is a word part on the front. Un- means not, so unhappy is not happy. A **suffix** is a word part on the end. -ful means full of, so joyful is full of joy. Underneath is the **root**, the main part carrying the meaning.

Now the honest part. Sometimes there is no clue at all. The sentence gives you nothing, and guessing harder will not help. That is the moment to ask someone or use a dictionary. Knowing when to stop guessing is a reading skill too.
to:
## The Words Around the Word

Read this: *The path was so narrow that we had to walk single file.*

Suppose you did not know **narrow**. You would still have a good guess. If people have to walk one behind the other, the path is probably not wide. You did not look anything up. The sentence told you.

That is what a **context** **clue** is. The words around a word hint at what it means. You can practice this strategy with support.

There are four kinds worth knowing by name.

Sometimes the writer just tells you. *A glacier, a large mass of ice formed on land that moves under its own weight, carved this valley.* That is a **definition** clue, and it gives the meaning directly.

Sometimes you get cases instead. *She packed produce: apples, carrots, and lettuce.* Nobody defined produce, but the **example** clue shows you it means fruits and vegetables.

Sometimes a nearby word means almost the same thing. *He was furious. I had never seen him so angry.* Angry is a **synonym**, and it hands you the meaning.

Sometimes the sentence swings the other way. *The room was not tidy; it was a shambles.* The little word not tells you a shambles is the opposite of tidy. That is an **antonym** clue.

Watch for **signal** words. Or, that is, and such as often bring a definition or an example. But, however and instead can introduce a contrast.

The word itself can help too. A **prefix** is a word part on the front. Un- means not, so unhappy is not happy. A **suffix** is a word part on the end. -ful means full of, so joyful is full of joy. Underneath is the **root**, the main part carrying the meaning.

Now the honest part. Sometimes there is no clue at all. The sentence gives you nothing, and guessing harder will not help. That is the moment to ask someone or use a dictionary. Knowing when to stop guessing is a reading skill too.

The clue types can overlap. Name the clearest clue and explain the wording that supports it. A contrast is not always an exact opposite. Word parts provide another kind of help, separate from surrounding context. Do not remove arbitrary letters: unbreakable has un- + break + -able, but other words have different structures. A meaning that sounds plausible can still be wrong; check reliable explanations when uncertain.

from: A sentence that tells you straight out what a word means.
to: Words that directly tell what something means. They need not be a full sentence.

from: A word part added to the front that changes the meaning.
to: A meaningful part attached before a base, such as un- in unhappy.

from: A word part added to the end that changes the meaning.
to: A meaningful part attached after a base, such as -ful in joyful.

from: The main part of a word, the part that carries its meaning.
to: A part carrying core meaning. In unbreakable, break is the root and base.

from: A small word like or, but, or such as that tells you a hint is coming.
to: A word or phrase that can show a link, such as but, or or such as.

from: DEFINITION · it just tells you
to: DEFINITION

from: "A glacier, a huge slow river of ice, …"
to: "A glacier, a large moving mass of land ice, …"

from: EXAMPLE · it shows you cases
to: EXAMPLE

from: "produce: apples, carrots, and lettuce"
to: citrus: lemons, limes and oranges

from: SYNONYM · a word that matches
to: SYNONYM

from: ANTONYM · a word that flips it
to: CONTRAST / ANTONYM

from: AND WHEN THERE IS NO CLUE
to: CHECK OR LOOK UP

from: The root is the main part in the middle that carries the meaning.
to: A root carries core meaning; a base is a form to which a prefix or suffix can be added. Not every word has three parts.

from: Cover the ends with two fingers. Whatever is left is the root. Now take one finger off at a time. Ask what that piece did. Un-happy: cover un-, find happy, then put not back on.
to: Look at unbreakable. Find break, un- and -able. Together they mean not able to be broken. Cover or mark each known part.

from: Covering the ends turns a long scary word into a short familiar one. Uncovering them one at a time shows what each part changed.
to: Use parts that really belong to the word. Do not cut off random letters. Check whether the meaning fits the sentence.

from: Cover the ends and read what is left.
to: Mark known meaningful parts; ask for help if the split is uncertain.

from: What does the root mean on its own, before the parts go back on?
to: What does break mean in unbreakable, before the affixes are added?

from: Why is finding the root first easier than reading the whole word at once?
to: When does recognizing a familiar base help you understand a longer word?

from: A drought, which means a long time with no rain, hit the farms.
to: A drought, an unusually dry period with too little precipitation, hit the farms.

from: Nocturnal animals, that is, animals awake at night, filled the woods.
to: Nocturnal animals, that is, animals active mainly at night, filled the woods.

from: "A glacier, a huge slow-moving river of ice, carved this valley." Which clue is that?
to: "A glacier, a large mass of ice formed on land that moves under its own weight, carved this valley." Which clue is that?

from: That happens to everyone, and it is fine. Read the sentence again with your meaning in it. If it sounds odd, your guess was off. Trying and checking is the whole method.
to: Substitute your possible meaning and reread. If it does not fit, revise it. Even a plausible meaning may need checking in a dictionary or with someone who can explain.

from: Usually, but not always. Un- almost always means not. In- often means not, as in invisible, yet in include it does not. Check your guess against the sentence.
to: Prefixes can have different meanings. Un- means not in unhappy, but undo means reverse an action. Check the word parts and the sentence together.

from: Not really. A name does not have a meaning you can work out from the sentence. Sound it out, keep going, and let the story tell you who they are.
to: Context can tell you who a named person is and what they do, but may not reveal the pronunciation or name origin. Ask for a model rather than assuming you can decode every name.

from: A student had the word drenched and kept writing it means very wet.
to: A student needed an example clue for the category citrus.

from: She changed it to: He came in drenched, and a puddle grew under his coat. Her partner got it at once, and nobody had been told the meaning.
to: She wrote: We packed citrus such as lemons, limes and oranges. Her partner used the listed fruits to suggest a meaning, then checked it.

from: She showed the result instead of stating the meaning, which is what an example clue does.
to: The sentence lists members of a category. A result such as water dripping from a coat would instead support an inference about drenched; it is not the same kind of category-example clue.

from: A matching word in the next sentence
to: A matching word in the same sentence
